Methodology.summary: The paper uses a long context approach, where models are trained on a large corpus of text and then fine-tuned on a specific task, such as multi-document question answering. The models are often better at using relevant information at the beginning and end of contexts, but suffer degraded performance in the middle.

evidence.text: We use language models in a standard retrieverreader setup. A retrieval system (Contriever, finetuned on MS-MARCO) takes an input query from NaturalQuestions-Open and returns the k documents from Wikipedia with the highest relevance score. To condition language models on these retrieved documents, we simply include them in the prompt. We evaluate retriever recall and reader accuracy (whether any of the annotated answers appear in the predicted output) as a function of the number of retrieved documents k. The 7B models with and without additional fine-tuning show minimal primacy bias, and are largely recency-biased. The 13B base model has a dramatic primacy and recency bias—there is a 20-point accuracy disparity between the bestand worst-case performance. Applying additional finetuning to the 13B seems to slightly reduce this bias (10-point worst-case degradation), but the bias remains significant. However, the 70B models with and without additional fine-tuning have largely similar trends (showing both primacy and recency bias), and additional fine-tuning minimally changes the positional bias severity. 1st 5th 10th 15th 20th Position of Document with the Answer [table values omitted] Accuracy

(2023), who compare question answering performance when the relevant paragraph is placed (i) at the beginning of the input or (ii) a random position within the input. They find that encoder-decoder models have significantly higher performance when relevant information is placed at the start of the input context. In contrast, we study finer-grained changes in the position of relevant information. 2.2 Models We analyze several state-of-the-art open and closed language models.
